newsitem.title: FRANCE: INTERVIEW -New French pensions may take generation.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -New French pensions may take generation.

text.p: Private pension funds, which will be allowed in France soon under new legislation, could take a generation to catch on, says Jean-Francois Debrois, managing director of insurance company AGF.

"We shouldn't be under any illusion on the money these funds are likely to attract, especially because of French reluctance when it comes to payouts in annuities," Debrois told Reuters in an interview. "Everyone from market players to employees and employers will have to grow used to it," he said.

Legislation allowing the set-up of private pension funds in France alongside the state-backed retirement benefit system was adopted by parliament on February 25 and could clear the way for such funds to start business by the end of 1997.
For Debrois, one of the main obstacles will be reluctance on the part of the wage-earner to join a voluntary private pension scheme which involves locking up savings for a long time.

"He (the employee) will say to himself, 'My money is locked up, if I die before reaching retirement, it's lost'. And others will tell him small-time savers saw their savings ruined (by inflation) at the beginning of the century," he said.
"We're going to have to get used to the idea that it's a way of providing a top-up for retirement, that there are drawbacks and risks, but also advantages -- and that will take years."

Asked how long he sees it all taking, Debrois replied: "A generation -- for those who have lived with pension funds, those who join companies today or who have joined not so long ago, it will become something normal."

Debrois believes that this phenomenon makes it difficult to carry out simulations on likely fund activity, even if some in the business cite "ballpark" estimates of flows of 25-30 billion francs when the system reaches cruising speed.
"Nobody as far as I know has said just when they expect this cruising speed to be reached," he says.

Keeping things simple, says Debrois, "if you put away 1,000 francs a month from the age of 40 until 60, the return will be 1,000 francs a month from the age of 60, with a life expectancy of 20 years from that date".

This hypothesis, he notes, remains simple to the extent that it does not take into account a possible reevaluation in order to maintain purchasing power, nor fees and costs, nor the fact that life spans are growing by three months annually.

Moreover, this example does not account for contributions by employers, which the legislation allows for to the tune of four times an employee's payment, nor for the case where there is a lump sum withdrawal of the maximum 20 percent allowed.
"With each client, we could draw up more precise calculations . But if we keep it simple, I believe it amounts to that -- you get out what you put in," said Debrois.

Another key factor for the future of these pension funds will be the ability of companies to contribute to funds on their staff's behalf. "It's not just because there's a law on pension funds that companies will have greater resources," he said.
Debrois said he was not in favour of lump sum payouts, an idea pushed by some bankers when the law was being drafted.
"Our position at AGF has always been the following: we do not want yet another savings product because they exist already and the bankers have a lot more than the insurers," he said.
Concerning AGF's plans, Debrois said four working groups had been set up to study the creation of private pension funds.
But he noted that the publication of decrees dictating how the law applies in practice will take several months.
"We want to be among the leaders. The issue for us, whatever the size of the market, is to start from our own client base and the marketing base we have for this kind of product."
"We will have to define the marketing strategy, one at the global level and another at the individual level -- and all that in a market which is not going to be enormous."

Debrois declines to make forecasts on the level of business that can be expected. "We haven't worked on the idea of a market share, because doing that means you have to know the size of the market," he said.
